cards.q: What is an amine?
cards.a: A compound derived from ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
cards.why: The functional group of a primary amine is \(\mathrm{-NH_{2}}\).

cards.q: How are amines classified as primary, secondary or tertiary? What is a quaternary ammonium ion?
cards.a: By the number of carbon atoms bonded to the nitrogen: one (primary), two (secondary) or three (tertiary). A quaternary ammonium ion, \(\mathrm{R_{4}N^{+}}\), has four.
cards.why: This is different from alcohols and halogenoalkanes, where the classification depends on the carbon bearing the group.

cards.q: Classify this amine as primary, secondary or tertiary.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of diethylamine: a nitrogen atom bonded to two ethyl groups and one hydrogen.

cards.a: Secondary: diethylamine.
cards.why: The nitrogen is bonded to two carbon atoms (and one hydrogen).

cards.q: Is triethylamine, shown, a primary, secondary or tertiary amine?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of triethylamine: a nitrogen atom bonded to three ethyl groups.

cards.a: Tertiary: triethylamine.
cards.why: The nitrogen is bonded to three carbon atoms and has no hydrogens.

cards.q: True or false: 2-methylpropan-2-amine, shown, is a tertiary amine because the NH₂ is on a tertiary carbon.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-methylpropan-2-amine: a central carbon bonded to three methyl groups and an NH2 group.

cards.a: False. It is a primary amine.
cards.why: Only one carbon is bonded to the nitrogen. For amines, count the carbons on the N, not the groups on the carbon.

cards.q: Name this amine.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of butylamine (butan-1-amine): a four-carbon chain ending in an NH2 group.

cards.a: Butylamine (butan-1-amine).
cards.why: A primary amine is named from the alkyl group with “-amine”, or as an alkanamine with the position of the NH₂.

cards.q: Name this aromatic amine.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenylamine: a benzene ring with an NH2 group attached.

cards.a: Phenylamine
cards.why: An \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) group attached directly to a benzene ring.

cards.q: Identify the functional groups in paracetamol, shown.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of paracetamol: a benzene ring with an OH group on one carbon and, on the opposite carbon, an NH bonded to a C=O carbon that carries a methyl group.

cards.a: An amide (secondary amide, –NHCO–) and a phenol (–OH on the ring).
cards.why: An N bonded directly to a C=O is an amide, not an amine. Paracetamol is the painkiller sold as Panadol in Ghana and the UK.

cards.q: Name these two amides and say what is different about them.

figure.alt: Two skeletal formulae: ethanamide, CH3CONH2, and N-methylethanamide, CH3CONHCH3.

cards.a: Ethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONH_{2}}\) (a primary amide), and N-methylethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONHCH_{3}}\) (an N-substituted amide).
cards.why: “N-methyl” shows the methyl group is on the nitrogen, not on the carbon chain.

cards.q: How is ethylamine prepared from bromoethane? Give the reagent, conditions and equation.
cards.a:
Excess ammonia dissolved in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube (under pressure).
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} + NH_{4}Br}\)

answerFigure.alt: Bromoethane reacts with excess ammonia (two moles), in ethanol in a sealed tube, to give ethylamine, the ammonium ion and the bromide ion.

cards.why: The tube is sealed because ammonia is a gas and would escape on heating.

cards.q: Explain why excess ammonia is used when a primary amine is made from a halogenoalkane.
cards.a: To reduce further substitution.
marks: The primary amine product still has a lone pair on N, so it is also a nucleophile.
It can react with more halogenoalkane to form secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.
With excess ammonia, a halogenoalkane molecule is much more likely to meet ammonia than the amine.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ammonia with bromoethane to form ethylamine.
cards.a: Nucleophilic substitution, then a second ammonia molecule removes H⁺ from the ethylammonium ion.

answerFigure.alt: Two steps. Step 1: the lone pair on ammonia attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane and the C–Br bond breaks, giving the ethylammonium ion and bromide. Step 2: a lone pair on a second ammonia molecule removes an H+ from the N+ of the ethylammonium ion, giving ethylamine and the ammonium ion.

cards.why: Two moles of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) are used per mole of bromoethane: one as nucleophile, one as base.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethylamine with bromoethane to form diethylamine.
cards.a: Nucleophilic substitution by the lone pair on the amine’s nitrogen, then removal of H⁺ by another ethylamine molecule.

answerFigure.alt: Two steps. Step 1: the lone pair on the nitrogen of ethylamine attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane and the C–Br bond breaks, giving the diethylammonium ion and bromide. Step 2: a second ethylamine molecule uses its lone pair to remove an H+ from the N+, giving diethylamine and the ethylammonium ion.

cards.why: This is why a mixture of amines forms unless ammonia is in excess.

cards.q: Write equations to show how further substitution of bromoethane by ethylamine leads to a quaternary ammonium salt.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} + CH_{3}CH_{2}Br \rightarrow (CH_{3}CH_{2})_{2}NH + HBr}\)
\(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CH_{2})_{2}NH + CH_{3}CH_{2}Br \rightarrow (CH_{3}CH_{2})_{3}N + HBr}\)
\(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CH_{2})_{3}N + CH_{3}CH_{2}Br \rightarrow (CH_{3}CH_{2})_{4}N^{+}Br^{-}}\)
cards.why: In practice the \(\mathrm{HBr}\) reacts with amine present, forming a salt.

cards.q: What forms when trimethylamine reacts with bromomethane?
cards.a: Tetramethylammonium bromide, \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{4}N^{+}Br^{-}}\): a quaternary ammonium salt.

answerFigure.alt: Trimethylamine reacts with bromomethane to give the tetramethylammonium ion and the bromide ion.

cards.why: The nitrogen has no H left to lose, so the product stays as an ion: the substitution stops here.

cards.q: What are quaternary ammonium salts used for, and why?
cards.a: As cationic surfactants, in fabric softeners and hair conditioners.
cards.why: Those with a long hydrocarbon chain have a positive head that is attracted to negatively charged surfaces of wet fibres and hair, coating them and reducing static.

cards.q: What forms when butylamine reacts with bromoethane?
cards.a: N-ethylbutylamine (N-ethylbutan-1-amine), a secondary amine, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NHCH_{2}CH_{3}}\), and \(\mathrm{HBr}\). Further substitution can give tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.

answerFigure.alt: Butylamine reacts with bromoethane to give the secondary amine N-ethylbutylamine and hydrogen bromide.

cards.why: The lone pair on the nitrogen of butylamine makes it a nucleophile.

cards.q: How is a primary amine made from a nitrile? Give reagents and the equation for ethanenitrile.
cards.a:
Reduce with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) in dry ether (or hydrogen with a nickel catalyst).
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CN + 4[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\)

answerFigure.alt: Ethanenitrile is reduced by lithium tetrahydridoaluminate in dry ether to ethylamine.

cards.why: Hydrogen with a nickel catalyst (\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CN + 2H_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\)) is cheaper on an industrial scale.

cards.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of making a primary amine by reducing a nitrile rather than from a halogenoalkane and ammonia.
cards.a: Advantage: a single pure product. Disadvantage: more steps, using toxic cyanide.
marks: Advantage: there is no further substitution, so only the primary amine forms.
Disadvantage: making the nitrile needs \(\mathrm{KCN}\), which is very toxic, and adds an extra step (lower overall yield).

cards.q: Give a two-step synthesis of propylamine, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\), from bromoethane.
cards.a:
1. \(\mathrm{KCN}\) in ethanol, heat under reflux: propanenitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN}\).
2. Reduce with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) in dry ether (or \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\)/Ni): propylamine.
cards.why: The nitrile route adds one carbon atom to the chain.

cards.q: How is phenylamine made from nitrobenzene? Give the reagents, conditions and equation.
cards.a:
Heat under reflux with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, then add excess \(\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}\).
\(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}NO_{2} + 6[H] \rightarrow C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2} + 2H_{2}O}\)

answerFigure.alt: Nitrobenzene is reduced by tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide, to phenylamine.

cards.why: Tin and acid are the reducing agent, shown as [H].

cards.q: Why is sodium hydroxide added after reducing nitrobenzene with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid?
cards.a: To release the free amine from its salt.
marks: In the acid, phenylamine is protonated to the phenylammonium ion, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+}}\).
Excess \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) removes the proton: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+} + OH^{-} \rightarrow C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2} + H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: What are aromatic amines such as phenylamine used to manufacture?
cards.a: Dyes.
cards.why: Phenylamine is made by nitrating benzene and then reducing the nitro group.

cards.q: Why do amines act as bases?
cards.a: The lone pair on the nitrogen can accept a proton (\(\mathrm{H^{+}}\)): amines are proton acceptors.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{RNH_{2} + H^{+} \rightarrow RNH_{3}^{+}}\)

cards.q: Write an equation for butylamine reacting with water, and say why the solution is alkaline.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{3}^{+} + OH^{-}}\)

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of butylamine (butan-1-amine): a four-carbon chain ending in an NH2 group.

cards.why: It forms \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions. It is a weak base: the equilibrium lies to the left.

cards.q: Are amines strong or weak bases?
cards.a: Weak bases: they are only partially protonated in water.
cards.why: Their aqueous solutions are alkaline, but less so than sodium hydroxide of the same concentration.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of butylamine with hydrochloric acid and name the product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2} + HCl \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}}\)
Butylammonium chloride.

answerFigure.alt: Butylamine reacts with hydrogen chloride to give the butylammonium ion and the chloride ion.

cards.why: The salt is ionic, white and soluble in water. Adding a strong base, such as NaOH, releases the amine again.

cards.q: Put ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine in order of base strength, strongest first.
cards.a: Ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine
cards.why: The more available the lone pair on N, the stronger the base.

cards.q: Explain why ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
cards.a: The ethyl group pushes electron density onto the nitrogen.
marks: An alkyl group is electron-releasing (positive inductive effect).
It increases the electron density on the nitrogen, so the lone pair is more available.
The lone pair accepts a proton more readily.

cards.q: Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia.
cards.a: The lone pair on the nitrogen is partly delocalised into the benzene ring.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenylamine: a benzene ring with an NH2 group attached.

marks: The lone pair on N overlaps with the delocalised \(\pi\) system of the ring.
This lowers the electron density on the nitrogen, so the lone pair is less available.
It accepts a proton less readily than ammonia’s lone pair does.

cards.q: The \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) values of the conjugate acids are: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{3}^{+}}\) 10.8, \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) 9.3, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+}}\) 4.6. What do they show about the bases?
cards.a: The higher the \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) of the conjugate acid, the stronger the base: ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine.
cards.why: A high \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) means the conjugate acid holds on to its proton: the base binds \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) strongly.

cards.q: True or false: phenylamine is a stronger base than ammonia because the benzene ring, like an alkyl group, releases electrons.
cards.a: False. Phenylamine is the weaker base.
cards.why: The nitrogen lone pair is drawn into the delocalised ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.

cards.q: Describe what you see when butylamine is added to copper(II) sulfate solution, a little at a time and then in excess.
cards.a: First a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms; in excess it dissolves to give a deep blue solution of a complex ion.
cards.why: The amine’s solution contains \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), which precipitates \(\mathrm{Cu(OH)_{2}}\); then butylamine molecules replace water ligands, using their lone pairs, as ammonia does.

cards.q: Write an equation for the formation of the deep blue complex when excess butylamine reacts with hexaaquacopper(II) ions.
cards.why: Butylamine is a monodentate ligand: the nitrogen donates its lone pair to the copper ion, forming a dative bond.

cards.q: Why are ammonia and amines nucleophiles?
cards.a: The nitrogen has a lone pair it can donate to an electron-deficient (\(\delta+\)) carbon, forming a new covalent bond.
cards.why: A nucleophile is an electron pair donor.

cards.q: What forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with concentrated ammonia? Give the equation and what you would see.
cards.a: Ethanamide: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONH_{2} + HCl}\). A violent reaction at room temperature, with white fumes.

answerFigure.alt: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ammonia to give ethanamide and hydrogen chloride.

cards.why: With excess ammonia: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONH_{2} + NH_{4}Cl}\). The white smoke is ammonium chloride.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ammonia with ethanoyl chloride.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination.

answerFigure.alt: Addition–elimination. A lone pair on ammonia attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon of ethanoyl chloride while the C=O π bond breaks onto oxygen. In the intermediate, the O− lone pair reforms C=O, the C–Cl bond breaks to give Cl−, and an N–H bond breaks to release H+. Products: ethanamide and HCl.

cards.why: Four arrows: lone pair to C; C=O to O; O⁻ reforms C=O as C–Cl breaks; N–H to N, losing \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) (removed by \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) or another \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)).

cards.q: What forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine? Give the equation.
cards.a: N-methylethanamide: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + CH_{3}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{3} + HCl}\)

answerFigure.alt: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine to give N-methylethanamide and hydrogen chloride.

cards.why: With two moles of amine the second takes the \(\mathrm{HCl}\): \(\mathrm{CH_{3}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}}\) forms.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of methylamine with ethanoyl chloride.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination, forming N-methylethanamide.

answerFigure.alt: Addition–elimination. The lone pair on the nitrogen of methylamine attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon of ethanoyl chloride while the C=O π bond breaks onto oxygen. In the intermediate, the O− lone pair reforms C=O, the C–Cl bond breaks, and an N–H bond breaks to release H+. Products: N-methylethanamide and HCl.

cards.why: The arrow must start from the lone pair on N and end at the carbonyl carbon, not at the oxygen.

cards.q: Butylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride. Name the organic product and write the equation.
cards.a: N-butylethanamide: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2} + CH_{3}COCl \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{3} + HCl}\)

answerFigure.alt: Butylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride to give N-butylethanamide and hydrogen chloride.

cards.why: The amine’s N becomes bonded to the acyl group: a secondary (N-substituted) amide.

cards.q: What forms when ethanoic anhydride reacts with ammonia?
cards.a: Ethanamide and ethanoic acid: \(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CO)_{2}O + NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONH_{2} + CH_{3}COOH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Ethanoic anhydride reacts with ammonia to give ethanamide and ethanoic acid.

cards.why: An anhydride reacts like an acyl chloride but more slowly, and the by-product is a carboxylic acid, not HCl.

cards.q: Write the equation for ethanoic anhydride reacting with ethylamine, and name the organic products.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CO)_{2}O + CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{2}CH_{3} + CH_{3}COOH}\)
N-ethylethanamide and ethanoic acid.
cards.why: Primary amines react with acid anhydrides to give N-substituted amides.

cards.q: Which acyl chloride and which amine would you use to make N-ethylpropanamide, shown?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of N-ethylpropanamide: a three-carbon chain whose C=O carbon is bonded to an NH that carries an ethyl group.

cards.a: Propanoyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}COCl}\), and ethylamine, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\).
cards.why: Split the amide at the C–N bond: the C=O side comes from the acyl chloride, the N side from the amine.

cards.q: True or false: ethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONH_{2}}\), is an amine because it contains an \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) group.
cards.a: False. It is an amide.
cards.why: In an amide the nitrogen is bonded to a carbonyl carbon (C=O). Amides are not basic like amines.

cards.q: A student wants to make ethylamine and uses an excess of bromoethane with ammonia. What goes wrong?
cards.a: Further substitution: the product is mostly secondary and tertiary amines and the quaternary ammonium salt.
cards.why: Excess ammonia, not excess halogenoalkane, favours the primary amine.

cards.q: Name this nitrile, and the amine formed when it is reduced.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of propanenitrile: a two-carbon chain bonded to a carbon that is triple-bonded to nitrogen.

cards.a: Propanenitrile; reduction gives propylamine (propan-1-amine).
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{C{\equiv}N}\) carbon is counted in the chain, so the amine has three carbons.

cards.q: Which of these is the amine and which is the amide: ethylamine or ethanamide? Draw both.
cards.a: Ethylamine, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\), is the amine; ethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONH_{2}}\), is the amide.

answerFigure.alt: Two skeletal formulae: ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2, and ethanamide, CH3CONH2, which has a C=O next to the NH2.

cards.why: The names differ by the C=O: “-amide” has one, “-amine” does not.

cards.q: Name this amine, made from bromoethane and excess ammonia.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of ethylamine: a two-carbon chain ending in an NH2 group.

cards.a: Ethylamine (ethanamine).
cards.why: A primary amine with a two-carbon alkyl group.
